SRS11-P1-1.solved: Final paragraph states the undertaking directly: "What she had undertaken was not to decide whether the letters should arrive. It was to wait until she was asked a second time," and para 3 gives the promise and that "he had not asked again."
SRS11-P1-1.note: B/C/D/E are, respectively, the 'habit' reading and the three village theories the passage has already attributed to named villagers and then undercut ('None of the three had been in the sorting room'). Well-built: every wrong option is textually present but sourced to someone the passage discredits.

SRS11-P1-2.solved: Para 1: the envelope is laid in the drawer under the scales in December, then "In January she took it out again and put it in a tin ... on the shelf above the stove." 'Eventually' picks the tin, not the drawer.
SRS11-P1-2.note: C is the good distractor (the drawer is the intermediate resting place); the stem's 'eventually' is what separates them and it is doing real work.

SRS11-P1-3.solved: The clause itself: "a strange, lawyerly way of speaking for a man she had never heard use a word of more than two syllables." The oddity she registers is the mismatch between the diction and the speaker.
SRS11-P1-3.note: E ('written out beforehand and learned them') is the only near-miss and it is an outside assumption the passage never touches; it is a fair distractor precisely because it is the explanation a student supplies for themselves.

SRS11-P1-4.solved: Para 2 is hearsay from three villagers; para 3 opens "None of the three had been in the sorting room on the morning Bryn Cadoc came in," then narrates the scene from Ottilie's own recollection. The contrast is hearsay vs. an account from a person present.
SRS11-P1-4.note: The opening sentence of para 3 is close to a giveaway for this item once a student notices it, but that is the passage doing its job, not a tell. C ('back to before Ottilie's time') is weak - nothing supports it.

SRS11-P1-5.solved: "Thirty-one Decembers is a long while ... Ottilie had had leisure to consider that the promise had been a foolish one" - the sentence is about elapsed time, and 'had had leisure to' = had had ample time to.
SRS11-P1-5.note: C (freedom from employment) and B (ease of mind) are both live dictionary senses of 'leisure' and both are refuted only by the sentence's own time frame. This is a correctly built VIC item.

SRS11-P2-1.solved: Para 2 defines the shrinkage instrument: a cast made from a mould taken off another cast is smaller a second time. Para 3: sixty-one "sat a further step down." So sixty-one are second-generation - moulded off other casts.
SRS11-P2-1.note: See leakage report: this key and SRS11-P2-3's key are the same proposition stated twice.

SRS11-P2-2.solved: Para 3: "Every one of them had been bought between 1919 and 1923, and no cast bought in those five years fell into the other group."
SRS11-P2-2.note: A, B and D name properties the passage never mentions at all (rooms, handwriting, colour) - a student cannot reach them by any wrong path, only by not reading. E is the only distractor with a route to it.

SRS11-P2-3.solved: Para 4: moulding shop flooded in 1918 and out of use four years, yet the 1920 catalogue is the largest ever issued. "A workshop that is selling more heads than it can mould must be getting them from somewhere."
SRS11-P2-3.note: B overreaches on 'for good' - the flood was four years, and the 145 first-generation casts span 1908-1931. D and E are constructible but unsupported.

SRS11-P2-4.solved: Last para: the curator's complaint "was minuted, thanked, and not acted upon," it was "the only contemporary notice of a difference that anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers at any time in the seventy years that followed," and "Vass says so twice." The repetition is the tone marker.
SRS11-P2-4.note: B is well made and specifically refuted: para 4's 'what the Institute could not have known' would support it, but the stem restricts to the LAST paragraph, where the point is that they COULD have checked with callipers. A is the hedged 'declines to adjudicate' option and is not the key - correct, since 'Vass says so twice' is an adjudication.

SRS11-P2-5.solved: "they answer to one another closely but not to the rest" - the sixty-one match each other's measurements. 'Answer to' = correspond to.
SRS11-P2-5.note: C (reply to) and D (be responsible to) are the two idiomatic senses of 'answer to' that the context excludes; good spread.

SRS11-P3-1.solved: Nineteen days forward over twenty-two years, then three candidate causes are weighed: observer effort (11 of 19 days gained after the 2004 change to weekly walking), clearance (ruled out), and February temperature (real but confounded). "She cannot take her own boots out of it."
SRS11-P3-1.note: The key is an 'unsettled' option and it is the key - counted in the hedging tally. A, B, C, E are all flat contradictions of the passage rather than reachable misreadings, so the item is easier than its subject matter.

SRS11-P3-2.solved: Para 3: "In 2004 she began walking the heath weekly instead of fortnightly."
SRS11-P3-2.note: A, B, C are unmentioned; D is contradicted ('The route did not change'). Only D has any route to it.

SRS11-P3-3.solved: Para 4: if clearance were the driver the two cleared banks should have run ahead from 1999. "They did not. Cleared and uncleared come forward together, within a day or two of each other, in every year of the record after 1998."
SRS11-P3-3.note: A is the exact inversion and is the one strong distractor. Note the key's qualifier 'by itself' is load-bearing and correctly so - the dates DID come forward on the cleared banks, just no faster.

SRS11-P3-4.solved: Final para: "What she disputes is the use that has been made of her figure. Nineteen days has now appeared twice in print as evidence of a warming climate ... and she has written to both."
SRS11-P3-4.note: 'Irritation' is a shade hotter than the passage shows - she writes letters, she does not fume - but no other option survives, and the passage does say she 'disputes'. A is the hedged option and correctly not the key: she is emphatic about what the figure cannot show, she just declines to say what it does show.

SRS11-P3-5.solved: "A record of this kind ... is only as sound as the walking behind it" - the record's trustworthiness depends on the observation effort. 'Sound' = reliable.
SRS11-P3-5.note: B ('unbroken') is the best trap, since a continuous twenty-two-year record is exactly what this is; it fails because 'as sound as the walking behind it' is a claim about dependability, not continuity.

SRS11-P4-1.solved: Final para: "It was not modesty. It was that I did not want to be found out later in a claim I could not defend ... He was right and I was wrong, and the argument took ten minutes, which was nine more than it should have."
SRS11-P4-1.note: C ('pride in work she chose not to sign') is the reading the first four paragraphs set up and the last paragraph demolishes; E is refuted because the scholar tried to GIVE her credit. Strong set.

SRS11-P4-2.solved: Para 2: "He did not pay me in money. He paid me in books ... I could have the duplicates from his own shelves instead."
SRS11-P4-2.note: A and D are both reachable by half-reading para 2 ('did not pay me in money' / 'thirty pounds'), which is more than the usual SSAT detail item offers.

SRS11-P4-3.solved: Para 3: "He had not asked me first. He said it as a thing already decided, which was the way he said most things." Offering it as settled presupposes she would want it.
SRS11-P4-3.note: A ('making up for having paid her so little') is the nearest miss and a student can build it from para 2 - but the passage never connects the title page to the payment, and 'most strongly suggests' points at the explicit sentence. C is directly contradicted ('He argued for about ten minutes').

SRS11-P4-4.solved: "It was not modesty. It was that I did not want to be found out later in a claim I could not defend, and that is a thing you do for yourself and not for the book," plus "nine more [minutes] than it should have."
SRS11-P4-4.note: A is refuted word for word ('It was not modesty'); B is the hedged option and is refuted by 'He was right and I was wrong'. This is the best item in the form - each distractor is killed by a specific clause. Leakage: it shares its ground with SRS11-P4-1.

SRS11-P4-5.solved: "He was plain with me about it. He wrote that he had thirty pounds for the whole edition, that thirty pounds would not buy four hundred and eleven letters from anybody" - he was frank about the terms. 'Plain' = candid.
SRS11-P4-5.note: A, C, D, E are all genuine senses of 'plain'; only the 'plain WITH me' construction plus the disclosure that follows selects candid.

SRS11-P5-1.solved: Thesis stated twice: "when the lettering on a village war memorial goes shallow, the parish should leave it shallow," and "The wear is the one part of a memorial that cannot be commissioned."
SRS11-P5-1.note: B is the position the essay is written against; C/D/E are compromise positions the essay explicitly refuses (re-cutting at any depth by any mason is still replacement).

SRS11-P5-2.solved: Reached by elimination, not by a sentence. Para 2 records what was done: cut again "in the same face, in the same places, a good deal deeper than the original," with the result that "Ninety years of weather came off that stone in three days." Depth is the only one of the five options that names something the passage says actually happened.
SRS11-P5-2.second_defensible: E - 'the money could have been spent to better purpose'. The essay names the eleven hundred pounds twice and closes on 'Chaldon paid eleven hundred pounds to have its only irreplaceable feature taken off', which a student can fairly read as an objection to the expenditure. It is not the writer's objection, but the last sentence invites it.
SRS11-P5-2.note: WEAKEST ITEM IN THE FORM. The key misstates the writer's objection: he would object just as much to a re-cut at the ORIGINAL depth, because his complaint is that re-cutting removes the wear, not that the new letters are deep. 'A good deal deeper' is one incidental clause in a paragraph whose point is elsewhere. A student who has understood the essay perfectly can reject A on exactly that ground and then has nowhere good to go. Recommend rewriting the key to name the loss of the weathering, or rewriting the stem to ask what the writer says was DONE at Chaldon.

SRS11-P5-3.solved: Para 3 opens "I will allow one exception and it is narrower than it sounds," concedes the unreadable-name case, then narrows it: "That is not a licence to re-cut the memorial. It is a licence to re-cut a name."
SRS11-P5-3.note: A describes para 4, not para 3 - a well-placed distractor for a student who loses count of paragraphs.

SRS11-P5-4.solved: Para 4: "I do not think the parishes that do this are careless of their memorials. They are the opposite. They are tidy people" - against the whole essay's claim that what they do is wrong.
SRS11-P5-4.note: HEDGING TELL HIT: C is the both-sides option and it IS the key. Mitigated by the fact that B is the true 'cannot decide' option and is refuted, and that E is refuted by a sentence that begins 'I do not think'. A student picking C for its shape rather than for para 4 would get it right, though.

SRS11-P5-5.solved: "But the memorial's office is not to be legible" - what the stone is FOR, set against para 3's 'the one thing it was put up to do'. 'Office' = proper function.
SRS11-P5-5.note: Genuinely hard and correctly built: A (religious office) and E (position of authority) are both live senses, and 'the parish council is the corporation that owns the stone' two sentences later dangles the institutional sense in front of the student.

SRS11-P6-1.solved: Para 2-3 kill the Herron story (bar sockets outside, unshuttered window). Para 4: "A flagged floor sloped to a drain is what you would build for a dairy, and it is also what you would build for a retting and drying room for flax ... I could not tell you which it was, and I know of nothing short of a new excavation that would."
SRS11-P6-1.note: The key is an 'unsettled' option and it is the key - counted in the hedging tally. B is refuted (1974 lifting produced nothing), E is refuted (accounts begin 1851, after the flax), A is refuted (the story predates 1888 and went in 'without a question mark' - i.e. it HAD been in print unquestioned).

SRS11-P6-2.solved: Para 3: "It is flagged; the flags are laid to a fall of about an inch in seven feet; and at the low corner there is a drain."
SRS11-P6-2.note: A-D are four floor types none of which appears anywhere in the passage. Pure recall; no wrong path produces any of them.

SRS11-P6-3.solved: Para 2: "the jambs carry the sockets for a bar - on the passage side. A room barred from outside is a room for keeping things in. A family shutting themselves in would have wanted the bar on their own side."
SRS11-P6-3.note: C and D are the archaeologically literate wrong answers (the passage says the jambs are original, which forecloses both) - a good use of a five-wide option set.

SRS11-P6-4.solved: Last para: "the vault is bonded into the outer wall, course for course, and went up when the house went up ... it was wanted from the first."
SRS11-P6-4.note: A and E are exactly what 'bonded course for course' rules out; they are the right distractors for this inference. The stem's restriction to the last paragraph is doing real work.

SRS11-P6-5.solved: The writer treats the Herron story as disposed of: "The door is against it ... The window settles what is left of the story," and the age of the tradition is noted only to be set aside ('told in that form for as long as anyone has been asking', into the 1888 volume 'without a question mark').
SRS11-P6-5.note: D is the hedged option and is a deliberate, well-set trap: the writer IS unwilling to adjudicate - but between dairy and flax, not about the Herrons. A student who conflates the two questions picks D. Small reservation on the key's second clause: 'untroubled by how old it is' rests on tone ('without a question mark') rather than on a statement, so the key is slightly wider than the text. It survives because D, and everything else, is refuted outright.
